beats.headline: Why do lambdas require a single abstract method?
beats.subline: It is not just syntax sugar. The compiler depends on target typing to map your code cleanly.
beats.narration: Before Java 8, passing a simple piece of logic into a method required six lines of anonymous inner class ceremony. Lambdas changed that, but what actually makes an interface compatible with a lambda?

beats.title: Anonymous Inner Class vs. Lambda Expression

top.label: Legacy Java 7
points: Creates a separate class file on disk
Heavy visual noise obscures business logic

bottom.label: Modern Java
points: Compiler infers types from functional target

beats.narration: Sorting a list by length used to take six lines of custom inner class boilerplate. With lambdas, you write a single line of concise parameter-to-expression mapping.

beats.title: Anatomy of @FunctionalInterface

steps.explanation: Exactly one non-Object abstract method forms the Single Abstract Method target.
Default methods and static helpers provide implementation, so they do not count against the limit.
Abstract methods overriding public Object methods (like equals) are inherited by all classes and do not count.

beats.narration: An interface annotated with FunctionalInterface must have exactly one abstract method. Default methods, static helpers, and overrides of Object methods like equals do not count against this single-method limit.

beats.title: SAM Compiler Validation
beats.subtitle: How javac decides if an interface supports lambdas

nodes.label: Interface Candidate
nodes.detail: Target interface evaluated by the compiler

nodes.label: Filter Non-Object Methods
nodes.detail: Excludes default, static, and Object method signatures

nodes.label: Count Remaining Abstract
nodes.detail: Validates exact count of remaining abstract methods

nodes.label: Functional Interface Valid
nodes.detail: Accepted as a valid target for lambda expressions

beats.narration: When the compiler inspects an interface, it ignores default methods, static methods, and Object class overrides. If exactly one non-Object abstract method remains, it qualifies as a valid functional interface target.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
takeaways: Functional interfaces need exactly one abstract method (SAM)
Default, static, and Object overrides don't break SAM
@FunctionalInterface asks javac to enforce the rule

beats.headline: Why won't Java let you mutate local variables inside a lambda?
beats.subline: It is not an oversight. Java enforces this to prevent race conditions across threads.
beats.narration: Try mutating a local counter inside a Java lambda and your code won't compile. Java enforces this strictly to prevent subtle concurrency bugs.

beats.title: Lexical Scope: Anonymous Class vs. Lambda

top.label: Anonymous Inner Class
points: 'this' refers to the inner class instance
Can shadow local variables of enclosing class

bottom.label: Lambda Expression
points: 'this' refers to the enclosing outer object

beats.narration: Unlike anonymous inner classes, a lambda does not create its own lexical scope. Inside a lambda, 'this' points directly to the enclosing outer instance, and local variables cannot be shadowed.

beats.title: Stack Frame vs Heap Capture
beats.subtitle: Why Java copies primitive locals by value

nodes.label: Method Stack Frame
nodes.detail: Holds local variable threshold on execution stack

nodes.label: Value Copied to Heap
nodes.detail: Lambda object captures a copy of threshold value

nodes.label: Stack Frame Popped
nodes.detail: Method returns and stack frame memory is reclaimed

nodes.label: Lambda Runs on Heap
nodes.detail: Lambda reads its own safe copied value independently

beats.narration: Local variables reside in stack frames that disappear when methods return. Because a lambda might execute later on a different thread, Java captures local variables by copying their values onto the heap.

beats.title: Working with Capture Rules

steps.explanation: Assigned once and never changed in scope, allowing safe read access inside the lambda.
The reference 'counter' is final; mutating internal AtomicInteger state is safe across threads.
Instance and static fields reside on the heap and can be mutated via the captured 'this' reference.

beats.narration: You can read effectively final locals that are never reassigned. To track state mutations across lambda executions, use an AtomicInteger reference or update instance fields through the captured 'this' reference.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
takeaways: Lambdas share lexical scope with enclosing outer class
Captured local variables must be final or effectively final
Instance and static fields bypass local final restrictions

parts.partTitle: The 4 Types of Method References & NPE Pitfalls

beats.headline: Can a method reference throw a NullPointerException at declaration?
beats.subline: Bound instance references evaluate their target receiver object immediately.
beats.narration: Method references aren't just syntax sugar—bound method references can throw silent NPEs before execution.

beats.title: The 4 Method Reference Varieties

steps.explanation: ClassName::staticMethod maps parameters directly to static method arguments.
instanceExpr::instanceMethod binds to a specific target instance evaluated immediately.
ClassName::instanceMethod makes the first parameter the receiver target.
ClassName::new binds directly to object or array constructors.

beats.narration: Java features four method reference types: static methods, bound instance methods attached to a fixed target, unbound instance methods taking receiver as first parameter, and constructor references.

beats.title: Bound Reference Evaluation Trap

top.label: Bound Reference (Eager Evaluation)
top.code:
// Evaluates getLogger() IMMEDIATELY at creation time!
Consumer<String> logNow = getLogger()::info;
points: Evaluates left side immediately on creation
Throws NPE right away if getLogger() returns null

bottom.label: Explicit Lambda (Lazy Evaluation)
bottom.code:
// Evaluates getLogger() LAZILY when accept() is called
Consumer<String> logLater = msg -> getLogger().info(msg);
points: Avoids premature startup null pointer errors

beats.narration: Look closely at bound instance references. The target expression on the left of double colon is evaluated immediately when created. If it evaluates to null, it throws a NullPointerException right away.

beats.title: Inspecting Eager Reference NPE
beats.caption: Stack trace proves NPE happens during method reference creation

lines.text: # Compiling bound vs unbound lambda references

beats.narration: When running this code, notice the stack trace. The NullPointerException fires during method reference assignment, long before the functional interface method is ever called.

beats.title: Part 3 Locked In
takeaways: Method references come in static, bound, unbound, and constructor forms
Bound references evaluate the target instance expression immediately
Use lambdas when target expression evaluation must be deferred

beats.headline: Can Predicate<Integer> slow down your high-throughput stream?
beats.subline: Autoboxing primitives in tight loops creates heavy heap allocations and GC spikes.
beats.narration: Using Predicate Integer inside a loop processing millions of items creates massive garbage collection pressure. Here is how primitive specializations fix it.

beats.title: java.util.function Core Hierarchy
beats.subtitle: 4 core functional shapes power the standard library

nodes.label: Supplier<T>
nodes.detail: Takes zero args, returns T (produces value)

beats.narration: The standard library builds on four core functional shapes: Predicates for testing conditions, Functions for mapping values, Consumers for side effects, and Suppliers for deferred value generation.

beats.title: Eliminating Autoboxing Overhead

steps.explanation: Forces Integer.valueOf(n) for every primitive, allocating objects on the heap.
Accepts raw primitive int with zero object allocation.
ToIntFunction, LongConsumer, and DoubleSupplier pass unboxed primitive values directly.

beats.narration: Generic functional interfaces like Predicate Integer force autoboxing for primitive values. Primitive specializations like IntPredicate, ToIntFunction, and LongConsumer operate directly on primitives with zero heap allocation.

beats.title: Composing Logic Pipelines

steps.explanation: Combine checks with and(), or(), negate(), and Predicate.not() for clean readability.
f.andThen(g) executes f first, then passes result to g (left to right order).

beats.narration: Compose predicates easily using and, or, negate, and Predicate.not. For functions, andThen chains operations from left to right, creating clear declarative processing pipelines.

beats.title: Part 4 Locked In
takeaways: Master the core shapes: Predicate, Function, Consumer, Supplier
Use Int, Long, and Double specializations to eliminate autoboxing
Chain logic with Predicate composition and Function.andThen

beats.headline: Does javac compile every lambda into an inner class file?
beats.subline: No. Java uses invokedynamic and LambdaMetafactory to link lambdas at runtime.
beats.narration: Java lambdas do not compile into anonymous inner class files on disk. The JVM uses invokedynamic to dynamically link lambdas at runtime.

beats.title: Lambda Execution Pipeline
beats.subtitle: From Java source to high-speed CallSite execution

nodes.label: javac Compiler
nodes.detail: Extracts body to private synthetic method + invokedynamic site

nodes.label: Hidden Class Created
nodes.detail: HotSpot dynamically generates lightweight class in memory

nodes.label: Direct Execution
nodes.detail: Subsequent calls execute linked CallSite with zero overhead

beats.narration: At compile time, javac extracts the lambda body into a private synthetic method. On first run, invokedynamic invokes LambdaMetafactory to spin up a lightweight hidden class and link a high-speed CallSite.

beats.title: Disassembling Bytecode with javap -c -p
beats.caption: Inspecting generated synthetic methods and invokedynamic instructions
beats.narration: Disassembling the class file reveals two key secrets: javac created a private static synthetic method containing the lambda body, and generated an invokedynamic instruction referencing LambdaMetafactory.

beats.title: Handling Checked Exceptions in Lambdas

top.label: Direct Call (Compile Error)
points: Standard functional interfaces ban checked exceptions
Inlining raw checked calls causes compilation errors

bottom.label: Unchecked Helper Wrapper
points: Keeps functional stream pipelines clean and legible

beats.narration: Standard functional interfaces do not declare checked exceptions. Handle them by wrapping exceptions inside helper methods or UncheckedIOException to keep functional stream pipelines clean.

beats.title: Chapter Complete! Run the Lab
takeaways: invokedynamic and LambdaMetafactory link lambdas dynamically at runtime
Non-capturing lambdas are cached to avoid repeated allocations
Wrap checked exceptions in helper methods for functional interfaces
